report.headline: Usage rate projected to land right at the NBA average, but the efficiency projection is not trustworthy

projection.text: Usage rate is projected at 19.9% in the NBA, down from 26.1% in the source G League season, landing almost exactly at the target league's minutes-weighted average of 20.1%.

risks.text: The true shooting projection of 56.6% should not be relied upon: it is no more accurate than simply guessing the league average, since the model's 4.7% error ties the trivial baseline's 4.7% error on this metric.
The usage-rate estimate rests on only 45 historical G League-to-NBA transitions, a thin sample for a projection this specific.
Two full seasons passed between the source campaign and the actual NBA arrival, adding a gap the projection does not directly account for.

Only about 52.9% of a player's standing above the G League average on usage rate typically carries over to the NBA, per the fitted slope, so the large source-season role is not expected to translate proportionally.

strengths.text: Produced 25.374 points per 75 possessions on 63.7% true shooting in the source season, with the shooting mark sitting 1.42 standard deviations above the G League average.
Carried a 26.1% usage rate in the G League, 1.27 standard deviations above league average, indicating a primary offensive role rather than a marginal one.
Combined a 14.4% turnover rate with an 11.7% assist rate, a profile consistent with efficient, low-mistake scoring usage rather than high-risk playmaking.

uncertainty.text: The 80% prediction interval for usage rate runs from 14.5% to 25.4%, a span of about 10.9 points against a league standard deviation of 5.4% — wide enough that the model can rank this player among peers but not price him precisely. The true shooting projection of 56.6% carries no information at all, because the model's 4.7% mean absolute error is no better than the trivial league-average baseline's 4.7% error on that metric.
